title: Expected Shortfall, Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis
objectives: Compute expected shortfall from a small return series and contrast it with VaR
Explain why expected shortfall is called a coherent risk measure
Size a hypothetical stress scenario across a multi-asset portfolio
Distinguish stress testing, scenario analysis and reverse stress testing
motivation: VaR tells you where the tail begins, not what happens inside it, and regulators learned in 2008 that 'the loss level exceeded 1% of the time' says nothing about how bad those days are. Expected shortfall answers the question risk committees actually ask: *given* that we are having a bad day, what do we expect to lose? Stress testing then asks the complementary question: what if something happens that has never appeared in our data window at all?

blocks.text: Expected shortfall: the average of the bad days

blocks.caption: Expected shortfall at confidence $c$: mean loss conditional on exceeding VaR
VaR draws a line and reports the boundary. Expected shortfall walks past the line and averages the disaster: the tail behind the tail.

blocks.md: Expected shortfall exists because VaR answers the wrong question. VaR(95%) says: on 19 days out of 20, you lose less than X. It says *nothing* about the size of the loss on that 20th day, and a risk measure that is blind to exactly the days it exists for is a strange foundation. ES(95%) asks the follow-up: *given that we are in the bad 5% of outcomes, what is the average loss?* It costs more to compute (you need the tail, not a quantile) and it is what regulators moved to after 2008 for precisely that reason.

blocks.title: VaR vs ES on 20 hypothetical trading days
items: Daily P&L percentages, worst first: $-2.5, -2.1, -1.8, -1.6, -1.5, -1.2, \ldots$ (15 better days omitted).
**VaR90** = the 10th-percentile loss = 2.1%. "On 90% of days we lose no more than 2.1%." The 2.5% disaster day is invisible to this number.
**ES90** = mean of the worst 10% (worst 2 days): $(-2.5 - 2.1)/2 = -2.3\%$. ES > VaR always, and the gap *is* the tail information.
On a 10 million book: VaR90 says "210k", ES90 says "230k on average once you are already in the bad decade of days". The 40-point difference is the cheapest tail-risk education you will ever get.

Estimation honesty: with 20 points, the 95% tail contains *one* observation. ES95 is literally your single worst day. Reliable ES estimates need hundreds of tail observations, which is why practitioners bootstrap, fit parametric tails, or use filtered historical simulation instead of naive rolling windows.

blocks.md: Stress testing complements both measures by refusing to use the historical distribution at all. A stress scenario is a *specified* shock, equities −25%, credit spreads +300bp, correlation → 1, applied to today's book. Its value is that it can include events absent from your sample (the point of the exercise) and expose non-linearities that percentile statistics hide: the book that loses 2% in a −5% equity day may lose 9% in a −25% day once hedges saturate and gamma flips. VaR extrapolates your past; stress tests interrogate your imagination. desks that survived 2008 ran both.

blocks.title: ES is still a distribution-dependent number
blocks.md: Switching from VaR to ES does not fix estimation risk, it amplifies sensitivity to it, because the tail is the least-sampled region. An ES computed from 250 days of calm data is a calm-weather ES. Combine it with stress scenarios and backtesting (does the 95% measure actually breach ~5% of the time?) or it is decoration.

Worked on a \$1,000,000 portfolio with twenty clearly-hypothetical daily returns. Sorted worst-first, the relevant tail is: $-2.5\%,\ -2.1\%,\ -1.6\%,\ -1.4\%,\dots$ At 90% confidence, the worst 10% of twenty days is exactly the **two worst days**, so:

blocks.title: Historical 90% VaR and ES on the same data
items: VaR$_{90}$: the loss boundary of the worst 10%, the second-worst return, $-2.1\%$, i.e. \$21,000.
ES$_{90}$: the average loss across those two days: $(2.5\% + 2.1\%)/2 = 2.3\%$, i.e. \$23,000.
Interpretation: on a day in the worst decile, expect to lose about \$23,000 - more than the VaR quotes, because the average includes the single \$25,000 disaster.

blocks.md: ES is always at least VaR (it averages losses *beyond* the VaR level). Because it averages the whole tail rather than a single quantile point, it is sensitive to tail shape: fatten the worst day and ES moves while VaR may not budge. ES is **coherent**, it satisfies the axioms of a sensible risk measure, in particular *subadditivity*: the ES of a combined portfolio never exceeds the sum of the parts, so diversification can never look risk-increasing under ES. VaR violates subadditivity in some tail configurations, which is precisely why Basel moved market-risk capital from VaR to ES.

Stress tests skip likelihood entirely and ask 'what would this book lose under a specified shock?'. Hypothetical book: \$10,000,000 split 60% equities, 40% bonds with duration 6. Scenario: **equities fall 25%, rates rise 150 basis points**.

blocks.title: Sizing the stress loss
items: Bond leg: duration approximation $\Delta P \approx -D \times \Delta y \times V = -6 \times 0.015 \times 4{,}000{,}000 = -\$360{,}000$.
Compare with VaR-style numbers on the same book: a 95% daily VaR might quote \$15,000-\$25,000. The stress number is one to two orders of magnitude larger, that gap is exactly why both exist.

rows: Given a bad day, how bad on average?
What if this specific event happened?
Point loss for a named shock

blocks.md: Good scenarios combine shocks that historically occurred *together*: 2008-style (equities down, spreads exploding, correlations converging to 1), 2020-style pandemic, or hypothetical rate shocks the data window never contained. Naive scenarios shock one variable at a time and miss the compounding, in our worked scenario, if equity crashes and rate rise were perfectly independent in the model, the true combined loss would be understated because liquidity effects hit both legs simultaneously.

blocks.title: Complementary, not competing
blocks.md: VaR/ES describe the distribution your data *implies*; stress tests describe outcomes your data may not contain at all. A risk framework needs both: ES for daily limit monitoring, stressed scenarios for capital planning. When ES and stress numbers wildly disagree, investigate, it usually means the data window is too calm.

blocks.title: The probability trap
blocks.md: It is tempting to dismiss a 25% equity stress as 'impossible'. The right response is to note its conditional role: stress losses are not forecasts with dates attached, they are solvency checks. Capital must survive the scenario; *how unlikely* it is belongs to the capital-allocation discussion, not the risk-acceptance one.

guidedExercise.prompt: Using the same twenty-day dataset, suppose the single worst return worsens from $-2.5\%$ to $-4.5\%$ while all other returns are unchanged. Compute the new ES$_{90}$ in dollars and explain whether VaR$_{90}$ changes.
hints: VaR$_{90}$ was the second-worst return; check whether the second-worst changed.
ES averages the two worst losses.
guidedExercise.solution: Worst two are now $-4.5\%$ and $-2.1\%$. ES$_{90} = (4.5 + 2.1)/2 = 3.3\% \Rightarrow \$33{,}000$. VaR$_{90}$ stays at the second-worst return, $2.1\% \Rightarrow \$21{,}000$ - it is completely blind to the disaster day. This is the single cleanest demonstration of why tail-aware measures exist.

independentExercise.prompt: A \$5,000,000 portfolio is 50% equities, 30% bonds (duration 5), 20% cash. Stressed scenario: equities $-30\%$, rates $+200$bp, cash flat. (a) Compute each leg's loss. (b) Total stressed loss in dollars and in % of the portfolio. (c) The same portfolio's historical ES$_{90}$ is 2.2%. State the ratio of stressed loss to ES and what that gap represents.
hints: 20% of 5,000,000 sits in cash and moves not at all.
independentExercise.solution: (a) Equities: $0.5 \times 5{,}000{,}000 \times 0.30 = \$750{,}000$ loss. Bonds: $0.3 \times 5{,}000{,}000 = \$1{,}500{,}000$ exposed; $5 \times 0.02 \times 1{,}500{,}000 = \$150{,}000$ loss. Cash: \$0. (b) Total $= \$900{,}000$, i.e. $18\%$ of the portfolio. (c) Ratio $= 900{,}000/(0.022 \times 5{,}000{,}000) = 900{,}000/110{,}000 \approx 8.2$: the stress is over eight times the recent-tail average, evidence the data window contains nothing resembling this scenario.

commonMistakes: Treating ES as 'the worst loss', it is an average of tail losses, bounded above only by the data or scenario's extreme.
Reporting stressed losses as predictions with probabilities attached; scenarios are conditional what-ifs, not forecasts.
Shocking variables one at a time and adding the pieces, ignoring that real crises hit several legs simultaneously.
Assuming VaR and ES will be close; for fat-tailed books ES can be multiples of VaR.
realWorldApplication: Regulators run annual CCAR/stress-test exercises where banks must survive defined severe scenarios with capital intact; internally, funds run daily ES limits alongside quarterly board-level stress packs.
quantFinanceApplication: A risk system computes ES by averaging simulated or historical tail losses, and runs the scenario engine by applying shock vectors to stored sensitivities (duration, beta, vega), the arithmetic in this lesson is literally the production calculation.
summary: $ES_c = E[L \mid L > \text{VaR}_c]$: the average loss beyond VaR; always $\ge$ VaR and responsive to tail shape.
ES is coherent (subadditive), which is why regulators replaced VaR with ES for market-risk capital.
Stress testing sizes named shocks on sensitivities: duration $\times \Delta y$ for bonds, percentage shock for equities.
Stress numbers and VaR/ES numbers live on different scales by design, the gap measures how unrepresentative your data window is.

quiz.prompt: From the lesson's twenty-day data: worst returns $-2.5\%$ and $-2.1\%$, \$1m portfolio. ES$_{90}$ in dollars?
quiz.explanation: Average of the two worst losses: $(2.5 + 2.1)/2 = 2.3\%$ of \$1m $= \$23{,}000$.

quiz.prompt: The worst single day worsens sharply but the second-worst is unchanged. What happens to historical VaR$_{90}$ and ES$_{90}$?
quiz.explanation: Historical VaR$_{90}$ sits at the second-worst observation (unchanged), while ES averages the tail including the worsened day, so ES rises.

quiz.prompt: Stress test: \$10m book, 60% equities falling 25%, 40% bonds duration 6 with rates +150bp. Total loss in dollars?

options: It is always finite for bounded-loss portfolios
It is subadditive: combined portfolios never look riskier than the sum of parts
It never changes with new data
It respects diversification benefits even in the tail
quiz.explanation: Subadditivity is the defining axiom, and it guarantees diversification is never penalised in the tail, both (1) and (3) express this. (2) is trivially false: all risk measures update with data.

quiz.prompt: What question does a *reverse* stress test answer, and why is it useful to management?
quiz.modelAnswer: It asks what scenario would be large enough to break the firm (exhaust capital or breach a loss limit), solved backwards from the limit; it shows management the specific failure mode to defend against rather than a menu of arbitrary shocks.
quiz.explanation: Reverse stress testing starts from the outcome (insolvency or limit breach) and searches for the shock combination that causes it, focusing mitigation where it matters.

quiz.prompt: A \$5m book: 50% equities fall 30% in a stress; bonds and cash unaffected. Stressed loss in dollars?

flashcards.back: $ES_c = E[L \mid L > \text{VaR}_c]$ - the mean loss conditional on exceeding the VaR quantile.

flashcards.front: Why is ES preferred to VaR by regulators?
flashcards.back: ES is coherent (subadditive), reflects tail severity beyond the quantile, and never rewards diversification-destroying tail behaviour that VaR can miss.
Both size named shocks on sensitivities; scenario analysis usually means full coherent narratives (multi-variable), stress tests often single or combined shocks.
Solve backwards: find the scenario that exhausts capital or breaches the loss limit, then manage against that specific failure mode.
